analysis.one_liner: Shortens brand-name biologic drug exclusivity from 12 years to 5, allowing cheaper biosimilars sooner.
analysis.headline: The PRICED Act, a bipartisan bill to shorten brand-name biologic drug monopolies from 12 years to 5, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 18, 2022 and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologics are complex drugs made from living cells, and brand-name versions get 12 years of protection from cheaper copycat competition. This bill would cut that exclusivity period to 5 years, letting biosimilar makers enter the market years earlier and driving prices down through competition. To avoid disrupting drugs already on the market, it would apply only to biologics approved after the bill became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who rely on expensive biologics for conditions like cancer, arthritis, diabetes, and autoimmune disease. A shortened exclusivity window means biosimilars—cheaper versions of these drugs—could reach the market seven years earlier, and biosimilar competition has historically brought steep price discounts. Payers like employer health plans, Medicare, and Medicaid would also save, with some of the savings passed back to patients through lower cost-sharing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients on costly biologics and health payers

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Public Health Service Act to change the brand-name biologic exclusivity period from 12 years to 5 years, allowing biosimilars to be marketed much sooner [S2] [S3].

Earlier market entry by biosimilars creates price competition, and biosimilars typically sell at significant discounts to the reference brand product, lowering drug costs for patients, employers, and government programs [S2].
Conforming changes apply the same 5-year window to the related data and exclusivity provisions of section 351(m) [S3].
Applies only to biologic products licensed on or after enactment, so drugs already approved keep their existing protections, limiting market disruption [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers would lose roughly seven years of protected, monopoly-priced sales on newly approved products. Drug companies argue that exclusivity revenue funds the high fixed costs of developing biologics and that a 5-year window could discourage investment in new biological medicines, particularly those with modest expected sales.

drawbacks.text: Critics of shorter exclusivity periods argue that the revenue protected by the current 12-year window helps finance costly biologic research and development, and that cutting it to 5 years could reduce the incentive to develop new biologics [S2].
The bill applies only to future approvals, so patients taking existing expensive biologics would see no benefit until newly approved drugs went off exclusivity years after enactment [S3].

Exclusivity is only one barrier: patents, manufacturing complexity, and interchangeability rules can still delay biosimilar competition even after the exclusivity window closes, so actual savings could be less than the headline change suggests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a large potential benefit—earlier competition for a class of drugs that includes some of the most expensive medicines in the U.S.—at a cost borne by brand-name manufacturers and, indirectly, by some future R&D incentives. The transition-protecting structure (future drugs only) reduces disruption but also delays the benefit. A fair-minded skeptic can point to the R&D-incentive tradeoff, but the core bargain—seven fewer years of monopoly in exchange for faster price competition—comes down squarely on the side of patients and payers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 18, 2022, and the committee took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the PRICED Act in the House on May 18, 2022, joined by seven original cosponsors including one Republican [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
Ten members cosponsored the bill in total—9 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
No further legislative action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers are better off: they keep the 12-year exclusivity window and the monopoly-priced sales it protects, while patients continue paying brand-level prices for longer than under the bill. Patient groups and biosimilar makers, who supported faster competition, gained nothing from the bill's failure.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 18, 2022 and took no further action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan though lopsided—9 of 10 cosponsors were Democrats and 1 was a Republican—and no vote or floor action ever recorded a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have cut their exclusivity window from 12 years to 5 for future approvals, ending roughly seven years of monopoly-priced sales on new biologics. Under the current 12-year window, patients continue paying brand-level prices with no copycat competition.

The bill would let biosimilar makers enter the market seven years earlier for newly approved biologics, expanding their addressable market. Faster competition also means cheaper versions of drugs patients rely on.

industries.industry: Employers, insurers, and government health programs
industries.note: Earlier biosimilar competition lowers drug spending for Medicare, Medicaid, and employer health plans, and part of the savings typically reaches patients through lower out-of-pocket costs.
